stem: Which model of the Fast Track Land Reform Programme gave plots for small and medium commercial farming?

options.content: A2
options.rationale: Correct: A2 plots were intended for commercial farming.

options.content: A1 villagised
options.rationale: A1 plots are for household farming.

options.content: A1 self-contained
options.rationale: A1 plots are for household farming.

options.content: The communal model
options.rationale: Communal areas were not part of the models.

explanation: A1 was for small household farms; A2 was for small and medium commercial farms.

stem: What describes the villagised A1 layout?

options.content: Homes are grouped in a village, with fields and grazing around it
options.rationale: Correct: it is a nucleated pattern that makes services easier to provide.

options.content: Each family lives alone in the middle of its own farm, away from neighbours
options.rationale: That describes the self-contained layout.

options.content: Houses are strung out along a river only
options.rationale: That is a linear pattern.

options.content: All families share a single large farm
options.rationale: Each household had its own arable plot.

explanation: In a villagised layout homes are clustered in villages and arable plots are separate, with shared grazing.

stem: Which was a major reason for land reform in Zimbabwe?

options.content: Shortage of tourists visiting farms
options.rationale: Tourism was not the cause.

options.content: Unequal distribution of land at independence, with crowding in communal areas
options.rationale: Correct: this inequality was the main historical reason.

options.content: A fall in the number of people in rural areas
options.rationale: Rural populations were growing.

options.content: A requirement by the Lancaster House agreement to close all commercial farms in 1980
options.rationale: The agreement did not require closing farms.

explanation: Land was unevenly shared: the best land was mainly in large commercial farms and communal areas were overcrowded.

stem: Why did many new resettlement areas have problems of service provision?

options.content: Settlers refused to use schools and clinics
options.rationale: Settlers wanted these services.

options.content: Services were already complete on all former farms and ready for many more families
options.rationale: Farm infrastructure was designed for few workers and did not meet the needs of many households.

options.content: Schools, clinics and water points had to be built after households were settled
options.rationale: Correct: the services lagged behind the arrival of settlers.

options.content: There were no roads on any former commercial farm
options.rationale: Many farms had roads, though they were in poor condition.

explanation: Settlement happened faster than the provision of social services and infrastructure for many more households.
hints: Did the services come before or after the people?

stem: Which group faced a particular settlement problem when commercial farms were acquired?

options.content: A1 farmers, who were given houses in the town
options.rationale: A1 farmers were settled on the land.

options.content: Farm workers living in compounds, who lost jobs or housing in some cases
options.rationale: Correct: their employment and housing depended on the former farm.

options.content: Town councils, which received all farm workers as employees in the municipal service
options.rationale: There was no such arrangement.

options.content: Tourists on the farms
options.rationale: Tourists were not the group affected.

explanation: Workers on commercial farms depended on the farm for jobs and housing, so their position changed when ownership changed.
hints: Who lived on the farms but did not receive a plot?

stem: Why is secure tenure important for the development of resettlement settlements?

options.content: It removes the need for any services, since farmers can provide their own schools
options.rationale: Services are still needed.

options.content: It prevents anyone from moving
options.rationale: Tenure does not stop movement.

options.content: It makes farmers willing to invest and to borrow money using the land as support
options.rationale: Correct: investment in housing and farming needs security.

options.content: It reduces the need for roads
options.rationale: Roads are unaffected.

explanation: Farmers who are sure of their rights invest in buildings, boreholes and equipment and can use their land documents to access credit.
hints: Think about whether people invest in land they might lose.

stem: A former commercial farming district of 160 km² had 960 people before resettlement. After resettlement it has 320 households with 5 people each (illustrative data). Calculate the percentage increase in population density, to one decimal place.
explanation: Density before = 960 ÷ 160 = 6.0 per km². After: 320 × 5 = 1 600 people, so 1 600 ÷ 160 = 10 per km². Increase = (10 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100 = 66.7%. Giving 4 is the increase in density, not a percentage.
workedSolution: 1. Density before = 960 ÷ 160 = 6.0 per km². After: 320 × 5 = 1 600 people, so 1 600 ÷ 160 = 10 per km². Increase = (10 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100 = 66.7%. Giving 4 is the increase in density, not a percentage.
hints: Work out the density before and after first.

stem: A farming area of 16 000 ha is divided into 320 equal A1 plots. Calculate the average size of a plot, in hectares.
explanation: 16 000 ÷ 320 = 50 ha per plot (including grazing).

stem: A smaller A1 scheme of 12 000 ha has 240 households, each with 4.5 ha of arable land. What percentage of the scheme is arable land?
hints: First find the total arable area.

stem: A villagised A1 layout makes it easier to provide services than a dispersed layout.
explanation: True. Clustered homes mean that a school, clinic or borehole can serve many households within a short distance.

stem: The Lancaster House agreement of 1979 required land to be acquired on a willing buyer, willing seller basis during the first ten years of independence.
explanation: True. This limited compulsory acquisition in the 1980s, and resettlement was slower than many expected.

explanation: Communal areas were formerly called Tribal Trust Lands.
hints: The old name has the word 'Trust' in it.

stem: Explain why land reform took place in Zimbabwe.

points.description: At independence the best land with good soils and rainfall was mainly in large commercial farms, while most people lived on poorer communal land
Communal areas were overcrowded with soil degradation and landlessness
The liberation struggle created expectations of redistribution, and early resettlement was slower than expected

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At independence the best land with good soils and rainfall was mainly in large commercial farms, while most people lived on poorer communal land. Communal areas were overcrowded, with soil degradation and landlessness. The liberation struggle created expectations of redistribution, and early resettlement was slower than expected.

explanation: Inequality, pressure and expectations.
hints: Compare commercial farms and communal areas.

stem: Compare the A1 and A2 resettlement models.

points.description: A1 gave small plots for household farming, while A2 gave larger plots for commercial farming
A1 could be villagised (clustered homes) or self-contained, while A2 farms were dispersed with existing farm buildings
A1 aimed to relieve pressure on communal areas, while A2 aimed to create small to medium commercial farmers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A1 gave small plots for household farming, while A2 gave larger plots for commercial farming. A1 could be villagised or self-contained, while A2 farms were dispersed and often used existing farm buildings. A1 aimed to relieve pressure on communal areas, whereas A2 aimed to create small to medium commercial farmers.

explanation: Plot size, layout and aim.
hints: Think of size, layout and purpose.

stem: Explain two problems of service provision in newly settled areas.

points.description: Schools and clinics were built after the settlers arrived, so children walked long distances
Boreholes and water points were too few for the number of households
Roads and bridges built for a few commercial farms were in poor condition for many users
The government and councils had limited funds to build services in many places at once

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Schools and clinics were built after settlers arrived, so children walked long distances to school and sick people travelled far for care. Roads and bridges built for a few commercial farms were in poor condition for many users, and councils had limited funds to build services in many places at once.

explanation: Any two problems, each developed.
hints: Which services lagged behind the settlers?

stem: Suggest four ways of improving services and infrastructure in resettlement areas.

points.description: Build schools and clinics within walking distance, or provide transport
Drill and maintain boreholes and protect water sources
Repair and maintain roads and bridges to link farms to markets and growth points
Extend electricity and mobile coverage, possibly using solar systems, or plan rural service centres with markets, inputs and finance

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Schools and clinics could be built within walking distance or transport provided, and boreholes could be drilled and maintained. Roads and bridges could be repaired to link farms to markets, and electricity and mobile coverage extended using solar systems or the grid.

explanation: Any four valid improvements.
hints: Think of social services, water, roads and energy.

stem: Assess the effects of land reform on the development of rural settlements in Zimbabwe. [8]

points.description: Redistribution created new settlements and settled many households on former commercial farmland, increasing rural population density there
Villagised A1 areas have a clustered pattern, which makes services easier to deliver
New schools, clinics and boreholes were built over time, but early provision lagged behind the arrival of households
Roads and farm infrastructure were often in poor condition, and electricity was limited
New business centres and markets grew at junctions, while some existing centres lost the demand of former commercial farms
Farm workers in compounds faced loss of jobs or housing, and some moved to towns or informal settlements
Tenure security and access to credit affected investment in houses and farms
Judgement: the reform created many new settlements and extended land access, but the development of services and infrastructure lagged, so its effect has been mixed and depends on local conditions

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Land reform created many new rural settlements by settling households on former commercial farms, which raised population density there. In villagised A1 areas homes are clustered, so services are easier to deliver, but in dispersed self-contained and A2 areas they cost more. New schools, clinics and boreholes were built over time, but provision lagged behind the arrival of households, and roads and electricity were often inadequate. New business centres grew at junctions, while some existing centres lost the demand of former commercial farms, and farm workers in compounds faced loss of jobs or housing. Secure tenure and access to credit affect how much people invest in their houses and farms. Overall the effects on settlement development have been mixed: many more households have access to land, but services and infrastructure have developed slowly and unevenly.

explanation: Balanced assessment of effects on settlements, services and different groups.
hints: Cover settlement pattern, services, groups affected and a judgement.
